title: Basic Measurement Reactivity Simulation
text:
Model Setup
Let’s imagine we have the following model for a treatment we want to estimate for a prettest-posttest design:
\[ y_2 = \beta_0 + \beta_1 treatment + \beta_2 y_1 \]


Code
ggdag::dagify(y2 ~ y1,
              y2 ~ t,
              labels = dag_labels) |>
  ggdag::ggdag(use_labels = "label",
               node_size = node_size,
               text_size = text_size) +
  theme_void()









If we have measurement reactivity, the problem is that the act of taking the measurement at time 1 (\(y_1\)) acts as a confounder, meaning we can’t know if \(\beta_1\) might look different if \(y_1\) were not measured.
A standard solution might be to omit the prettest and just do a between-subjects comparison without any prettest as a covariate:
\[ y_2 = \beta_0 + \beta_1 treatment \]


Code
ggdag::dagify(y2 ~ t,
              labels = dag_labels) |>
  ggdag::ggdag(use_labels = "label",
               node_size = node_size,
               text_size = text_size) +
  theme_void()









One issue with this approach is that it is possible that baseline scores interact with the treatment, and that interaction becomes impossible to to measure. For example, it is possible that individuals with lower baseline scores may benefit more from the treatment than those with higher baseline scores, and this could not be measured with the just between-subjects condition.
\[ y_2 = \beta_0 + \beta_1 treatment + \beta_2 y_1 + \beta_3 (treatment \times y_1) \]


Code
ggdag::dagify(y2 ~ y1,
              y2 ~ t,
              y2 ~ y1_t,
              y1_t ~ t,
              y1_t ~ y1,
              labels = dag_labels) |>
  ggdag::ggdag(use_labels = "label",
               node_size = node_size,
               text_size = text_size) +
  theme_void()









Our approach uses a planned missingness design, where participants are randomized into a design where \(y_1\) measurements are either observed or missing, and Type B auxiliary variables are used to impute the missing values, eliminating the effect of measurement reactivity.
I sketched out a simple simulation with the following data generating model:

\[\begin{aligned}
  y_{2} = \beta_0 &+ \beta_1 treatment + \beta_2 prettest  + \beta_3 y_{1} \\
  & + \beta_4(treatment \times prettest) + \beta_5 (treatment_i \times y_{1}) + \beta_6 (prettest_i \times y_{1}) \\
  & + \beta_7 (treatment \times prettest \times y_{1}) + \epsilon_{y2}
\end{aligned}\]



Code
ggdag::dagify(y2 ~ u,
              y2 ~ y1 + t + pretest + t_y1 + pretest_t + pretest_y1 + pretest_t_y1,
              t_y1 ~ t + y1,
              pretest_t ~ pretest + t,
              pretest_y1 ~ pretest + y1,
              pretest_t_y1 ~ pretest + t + y1,
              labels = dag_labels,
              coords = list(x = c(u = 3.5,
                                  y2 = 3,
                                  pretest_t_y1 = 1.5,
                                  pretest_y1 = 0.75, pretest_t = 0.75, t_y1 = 0.75,
                                  t = 0, pretest = 0, y1 = 0),
                            y = c(u = 0,
                                  y2 = 0,
                                  pretest_t_y1 = 0,
                                  pretest_y1 = 0.75, pretest_t = 0, t_y1 = -0.75,
                                  t = -1, pretest = 0, y1 = 1))
              ) |>
  ggdag::ggdag(use_labels = "label",
               node_size = node_size,
               text_size = 4) +
  theme_void()










\(K\) is the number of auxiliary variables
\(N\) is the total sample size
\(treatment\) is the treatment condition (0 or 1)
\(prettest\) is the measurement condition (0 or 1)
\(y_1\) is prettest measurement
\(y_2\) is posttest measurement
\(n_{pre}\) is the sample size in the prettest condition
\(\beta_1\) is the effect of the treatment (compared to control) when there is no pretest at the average baseline score (\(y_1\))
\(\beta_2\) is the effect of the prettest being elicited on the posttest in the control condition (no target treatment) at the average baseline score (\(y_1\))
\(\beta_3\) is the effect of the prettest score on posttest (set to 1 for simplicity) in the control condition when there is no prettest
\(\beta_4\) is the difference in treatment effect (change in \(\beta_1\)) when the prettest is taken (vs when it is not) at the average baseline score (\(y_1\))
\(\beta_5\) is the change in the effect of the treatment (\(\beta_1\)) for one unit increase in baseline score (\(y_1\)) when the prettest is not taken.
\(\beta_6\) is the change in the effect of the prettest (\(\beta_2\)) for one unit increase in baseline score (\(y_1\)) when the in the control condition
\(\beta_7\) is the change in the change the effect of treatment for one unit increase in baseline score (\(\beta_5\)) when the prettest is taken
\(R^2_{aux}\) is the proportion of variance in \(y_1\) explained by auxiliary variables

The data generating process is based on
\[ \boldsymbol{aux} \sim MVN(\boldsymbol{0}, \boldsymbol{I}) \]
NOTE: for now this implies predictors are independent. We should manipulate this!
\[ y_{1,i} = \sum aux_i + \epsilon_{impute,i} \]
where \(\sigma_{\epsilon_{impute,i}} = K\frac{1-R^2_{aux}}{R^2_{aux}}\)






NoteRelationship Among \(\sigma\), \(K\), and \(R^2\)







Code
tibble(r2 = seq(.1, .9, length.out = 50),
       sigma = map(r2, \(r2) tibble(K = 1:5,
                                    sigma = K * (1 - r2) / r2))) |>
  unnest(sigma) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = r2, y = sigma)) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ K, nrow = 1, labeller = "label_both") +
  guides(x = guide_axis(cap = T),
         y = guide_axis(cap = T)) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Randomized Experiments

Behavioral research often deals with experiments where we want to test for positive benefits of some kind of experimental treatment
Examples:

Does a new medication improve mood?
Does a new type of therapy improve well-being?
Does an anti-smoking campaign increase likelihood of quitting?
Does a new math curriculum improve learning? (running example)


Core research design: Randomly assign participants to conditions:

Control
Treatment

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Between Subjects Designs

Simplest version of randomized design
Core model

\[
\widehat{\text{Math Score}}_i =\;
\underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{Control} \\ \text{Score}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_1 (\text{Treatment}_i)}_{\substack{\text{Treatment} \\ \text{Effect}}}
\]
Limitations

Statistical power
Does not allow for treatment effect to vary as a function of baseline ability (moderation)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Problem: Measurement Reactivity

What if the elicitation of the pretest itself acts as a confounding treatment?

Example: Exposure to math test might call attention to important study points
Goal of treatment is not to test how treatment helps pre-tested students, but how it helps students in general (typically who would not be pretested)

Makes the true population model:

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Math Score}_i =\;&
\underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{Control} \\ \text{Score}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\substack{\text{Treat.} \\ \text{Effect}}} (\text{Treatment}_i)
+ \underbrace{\beta_2}_{\substack{\text{Base} \\ \text{Score}}} (\text{Baseline}_i)
+ \underbrace{\beta_3}_{\substack{\text{Pretest} \\ \text{Effect}}} (\text{Pretest}_i)\\[1.5em]
&+ \underbrace{\beta_4}_{\substack{\text{Treat.} \times \\ \text{Baseline}}} (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i) + \underbrace{\beta_4}_{\substack{\text{Treat.} \times \\ \text{Pretest}}} (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i) \\[1.5em]
&+ \underbrace{\beta_6}_{\substack{\text{Pretest} \times \\ \text{Baseline}}} (\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i)
+ \underbrace{\beta_7}_{\substack{\text{Three-Way} \\ \text{Interaction}}} (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i)
+ \epsilon_i
\end{aligned}
\]

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
The Problem


When \(\text{Pretest}_i = 0\), that means \(\text{Baseline}_i =\) NA!
Measurement model cannot be estimated under normal conditions because anyone with an omitted pretest has missing data

Early solution

Solomon Four Group Design

Randomize participants into crossed \(2 \text{ (Treatment) } \times 2 \text{ (Pretest})\) design
Identifies but does not correct for measurement reactivity when present


New Contribution - Planned missing data design - Collect auxiliary variables - Impute missing \(\text{Baseline}_i\) values - Identifies and corrects for measurement reactivity

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Missing Data Mechanisms


\(\mathbf{Y}_{com}\): the hypothetically complete data, split into \(\mathbf{Y}_{obs}\) (observed) and \(\mathbf{Y}_{mis}\) (unobserved)
\(\mathbf{M}\): missingness indicator (1 = missing, 0 = observed)









Mechanism
Definition
Implication




MCAR  Missing Completely at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1)\)
Listwise deletion is unbiased, but wastes information


CMAR (MAR)  Conditionally Missing at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Must borrow information from observed correlates


MNAR  Missing Not at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) \neq P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Bias can only be addressed with strong assumptions

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
section: Measurement Reactivity as a Missing Data Problem
text:
Measurement Reactivity as a Missing Data Problem



Mapping to our example

\(Y_1 = \text{Baseline}_i\) (pretest score)
\(Y_2 = \text{Math Score}_i\) (posttest)
\(M_1 = 1 - \text{Pretest}_i\)


Measurement reactivity: the posttest depends on whether baseline was measured
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1) \neq P(Y_2 \mid Y_1)
\]
So we must separately model \(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 0)\) and \(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 1)\)

Planned missingness: we randomize \(M_1\) (the Pretest condition) independently of \(Y_1\)
\[
P(M_1 = 1 \mid Y_1, Y_2) = P(M_1 = 1 \mid \cancel{Y_1}, Y_2)
\]

Missingness may relate to \(Y_2\) (that is the reactivity), but never to the unobserved \(Y_1\)
Baseline is CMAR by design

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
What Can We Estimate?

\(M_1\) temporally precedes \(Y_2\), so the conditional of substantive interest runs the other way


Standard approach: drop \(Y_1\)  (akin to listwise deletion)
\[
P(Y_2 \mid \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]

✓ Treatment effect without pretest (\(\beta_1\))
✓ Measurement reactivity (\(\beta_3\), \(\beta_5\))
✗ Baseline effects and moderation (\(\beta_2\), \(\beta_4\), \(\beta_6\), \(\beta_7\))
✗ Power lost by ignoring baseline


Our goal: bring \(Y_1\) back
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]

✓ The full population model (\(\beta_0\) – \(\beta_7\))
✓ Greater power for treatment and reactivity effects
✓ Moderation by baseline, with and without a pretest

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Auxiliary Variables: Getting Baseline Back


Auxiliary variables (\(A\)): outside the focal model, but informative about missing values (Collins et al., 2001)

Type A: related to \(M\) and \(Y\) (critical in standard missing data problems)
Type B: related to \(Y\) only (improve precision and power)
Type C: related to \(M\) only (superfluous)

With planned missingness, \(M\) is set by randomization, so there are no Type A variables and Type B variables do the heavy lifting:

\[
P(Y_1 \mid \text{Pretest}, A) = P(Y_1 \mid A)
\]
The recipe

Learn \(P(Y_1 \mid A)\) from the pretested group
Impute the distribution of \(Y_1\) for the non-pretested group (maximum likelihood, multiple imputation, or fully Bayesian)
Estimate \(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})\)

Requirement: \(A\) must correlate strongly enough with \(Y_1\) to make the imputation informative (e.g., prior-year math grades, without exposing students to the test material)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
{.r-fit-text} Missing Data Mechanisms


\(\mathbf{Y}_{com}\): the hypothetically complete data, split into \(\mathbf{Y}_{obs}\) (observed) and \(\mathbf{Y}_{mis}\) (unobserved)
\(\mathbf{M}\): missingness indicator (1 = missing, 0 = observed)









Mechanism
Definition
Implication




MCAR  Missing Completely at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1)\)
Listwise deletion is unbiased, but wastes information


CMAR  Conditionally Missing at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Must borrow information from observed correlates


MNAR  Missing Not at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) \neq P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Bias can only be addressed with strong assumptions

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Reactivity as Missing Data



Mapping to our example

\(Y_1 = \text{Baseline}_i\) (pretest score)
\(Y_2 = \text{Math Score}_i\) (posttest)
\(M_1 = 1 - \text{Pretest}_i\)


Measurement reactivity: the posttest depends on whether baseline was measured
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 1) \neq P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 0)
\]
So we must separately model:

\(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 0)\)
\(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1 = 1)\)


Planned missingness: Randomize \(M_1\) (the Pretest condition) independently of \(Y_1\)
\[
P(M_1 = 1 \mid Y_1, A) = P(M_1 = 1)
\]

\(M_1\) is related to \(Y_2\), but as a cause of \(Y_2\), not a selection mechanism
We model it directly with the pretest terms in the measurement model
Missingness is fully determined by pretest condition. Baseline is MCAR by design

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Auxiliary Variables


Auxiliary variables (\(A\)): Outside measurement model, but informative about missing \(Y_1\)
The joint model factors into two pieces, estimated together:

\[
P(Y_2, Y_1 \mid A, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}) =
\underbrace{P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})}_{\text{Measurement model}}
\times
\underbrace{P(Y_1 \mid A)}_{\text{Imputation model}}
\]

Missing \(Y_1\) are drawn from plausible values given both \(A\) and \(Y_2\):

\[
P(Y_{1,\text{mis}} \mid Y_2, A, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}) \;\propto\;
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}) \times P(Y_1 \mid A)
\]

Randomization \(\Rightarrow\) \(P(Y_1 \mid A)\) is the same in both Pretest groups, so the pretested group shows how \(A\) predicts \(Y_1\)
Requirements: \(A\) is unaffected by the pretest (e.g., measured before randomization), relates to \(Y_2\) only through \(Y_1\), and correlates strongly enough with \(Y_1\) to be informative

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
What Can We Do?



Measure \(Y_1\) only when \(\text{Pretest}_i = 1\) (Solomon Four Group Design)
\[
P(Y_2 \mid \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]
Benefits:

Treatment effect without pretest (\(\beta_1\))
Can test for measurement reactivity (\(\beta_3\), \(\beta_5\))

Limitations:

Statistically just a lower-powered between subjects design if measurement reactivity is present

No more moderation
Weaker statistical power



Our goal: bring \(Y_1\) back
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]
Benefits:

Estimate full measurement model (\(\beta_0\) – \(\beta_7\))
Greater power for treatment and reactivity effects
Reintroduces moderation effects with baseline

Limitations

How do we estimate \(Y_1\)?

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Three Ways to Recover Baseline



Maximum Likelihood
mdmb::frm_em()
How it works:

Measurement model + model for Baseline written as one factored likelihood
Missing Baselines are integrated over, never filled in
Estimated with maximum likelihood (EM algorithm)

Inference:

Standard errors, \(p\)-values, confidence intervals (NHST)

Use when:

One model of interest and frequentist reporting
Interactions with an incomplete predictor (standard FIML in SEM software struggles here)


Multiple Imputation
Blimp via rblimp, pooled with mitml
How it works:

Bayesian MCMC (factored regression) draws \(m\) plausible Baselines for each non-pretested participant
Measurement model fit to each completed dataset with OLS
Results pooled with Rubin’s rules

Inference:

Pooled estimates, standard errors, \(p\)-values (NHST)

Use when:

You want complete datasets to reuse across analyses or software
Imputation model must include the outcome and interactions


Fully Bayesian
brms with mi(), Stan via cmdstanr
How it works:

Measurement model and model for Baseline estimated jointly in one model
Missing Baselines are parameters with their own posterior
One joint likelihood + priors → posterior for everything

Inference:

Posterior distributions, credible intervals, posterior probabilities

Use when:

You prefer Bayesian inference or want informative priors
Uncertainty about missing values carried through in one step


All three use the same information (A, Math Score, and the measurement model), so all three should recover \(\beta_0\)–\(\beta_7\)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Simulation Design

\[
\widehat{\text{Math Score}}_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{Treatment}_i) + \beta_2 (\text{Baseline}_i) + \beta_3 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i) + \beta_4 (\text{Pretest}_i) \\[1em]
+ \underbrace{\beta_5 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)}_{\text{Manipulated}} + \beta_6 (\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i) + \underbrace{\beta_7 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i)}_{\text{Manipulated}}
\]
\[
A_{ik} \sim N(0, 1), \qquad
\text{Baseline}_i = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} A_{ik} + \varepsilon_i}{\sqrt{K + \sigma_{B}^2}}, \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N(0, \sigma_{B}^2)
\]

\(N =\) 600, \(K =\) 3 auxiliary variables, \(R^2_{A} =\) 0.33
\(P(\text{Pretest}_i = 1) =\) 0.33, \(P(\text{Treatment}_i = 1) =\) 0.5
\(\beta_0 =\) 0, \(\beta_1 =\) 0.3, \(\beta_2 =\) 1, \(\beta_3 =\) -0.1, \(\beta_4 =\) 0.2, \(\beta_6 =\) 0

Between subjects designs

Sacrifice power (larger: \(\sigma\), variance in \(\beta_1\) estimates)

Risk triggering measurement reactivity, biasing treatment effects

Permit varying levels of treatment effect by baseline/trait ability

Test optimal designs for statistical power
Validate on real world data

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Randomized Experiments

Behavioral research often deals with experiments where we want to test for positive benefits of some kind of experimental treatment
Examples:

Does a new medication improve mood?
Does a new type of therapy improve well-being?
Does an anti-smoking campaign increase likelihood of quitting?
Does a new math curriculum improve learning? (running example)


Core research design: Randomly assign participants to conditions:

Control
Treatment

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Between Subjects Designs

Simplest version of randomized design
Core model

\[
\widehat{\text{Math Score}}_i =\;
\underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{Control} \\ \text{Score}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_1 (\text{Treatment}_i)}_{\substack{\text{Treatment} \\ \text{Effect}}}
\]
Limitations

Statistical power
Does not allow for treatment effect to vary as a function of baseline ability (moderation)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
The Problem


When \(\text{Pretest}_i = 0\), that means \(\text{Baseline}_i =\) NA!
Measurement model cannot be estimated under normal conditions because anyone with an omitted pretest has missing data

Early solution

Solomon Four Group Design

Randomize participants into crossed \(2 \text{ (Treatment) } \times 2 \text{ (Pretest})\) design


\[
\widehat{\text{Math Score}}_i =\;
\underbrace{\beta_0}_{\substack{\text{Control Score} \\ \text{No Pretest}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_1 (\text{Treatment}_i)}_{\substack{\text{Treatment Effect} \\ \text{No Pretest}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_4 (\text{Pretest}_i)}_{\substack{\text{Pretest Effect} \\ \text{in Control}}}
+ \underbrace{\beta_5 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)}_{\substack{\text{Difference in Treatment Effect} \\ \text{from Pretest} \\ \text{\textbf{(Measurement Reactivity)}}}}
\]

Identifies but does not correct for measurement reactivity when present

New Contribution

Planned missing data design

Collect auxiliary variables
Impute missing \(\text{Baseline}_i\) values
Identifies and corrects for measurement reactivity

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Missing Data Mechanisms


\(\mathbf{Y}_{com}\): the hypothetically complete data, split into \(\mathbf{Y}_{obs}\) (observed) and \(\mathbf{Y}_{mis}\) (unobserved)
\(\mathbf{M}\): missingness indicator (1 = missing, 0 = observed)









Mechanism
Definition
Implication




MCAR  Missing Completely at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1)\)
Listwise deletion is unbiased, but wastes information


CMAR (MAR)  Conditionally Missing at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Must borrow information from observed correlates


MNAR  Missing Not at Random
\(P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) \neq P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\)
Bias can only be addressed with strong assumptions

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Reactivity as Missing Data



(Conditionally) Missing at Random
\[P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs}, Y_{mis}) = P(M = 1 \mid Y_{obs})\]
Mapping to our example

\(Y_1 = \text{Baseline}_i\) (pretest score)
\(Y_2 = \text{Math Score}_i\) (posttest)
\(M_1 = 1 - \text{Pretest}_i\)


Measurement reactivity: the posttest depends on whether baseline was measured
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_{1, mis}, M_1 = 1) \neq P(Y_2 \mid Y_{1, obs}, M_1 = 0)
\]
Which implies:
\[
P(M_1 = 1 \mid Y_2, Y_{1, obs}, Y_{1, mis}) \neq P(M_1 = 1 \mid Y_2, Y_{1, obs})
\]
So we must separately model:

\(P(Y_2 \mid Y_{1,obs}, M_1 = 0)\)
\(P(Y_2 \mid Y_{1,mis}, M_1 = 1)\) (How???)


Planned missingness: make mechanism (C)MAR by randomizing \(M_1\) independently of everything measured before treatment.
\[
P(M_1 = 1 \mid Y_2, Y_{1, obs}, Y_{1, mis}, \text{Pretest}) = P(M_1 = 1  \mid Y_{1, obs}, Y_2, \text{Pretest})
\]

Then: find a way to impute missing \(Y_1\) from pre-treatment information, and model \(P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, M_1)\)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
What Can We Do?



Measure \(Y_1\) only when \(\text{Pretest}_i = 1\)
(Solomon Four Group Design)
\[
P(Y_2 \mid \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]
Benefits:

Treatment effect without pretest (\(\beta_1\))
Can test for measurement reactivity (\(\beta_5\))

Limitations:

Essentially between subjects analysis

Only based on \(\text{Pretest}_i = 0\) subsample
No more moderation
Lose statistical power vs. between subjects design



Our goal: bring \(Y_1\) back
\[
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
\]
Benefits:

Estimate full measurement model (\(\beta_0\) – \(\beta_7\))
Greater power for treatment and reactivity effects
Reintroduces moderation effects with baseline

Limitations

How do we estimate \(Y_1\)?

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Auxiliary Variables


Auxiliary variables (\(A\)): Outside measurement model, but informative about missing \(Y_1\)
The joint model factors into two pieces, estimated together:

\[
\begin{aligned}
P(Y_2, Y_1 \mid A, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})
&= \underbrace{P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \cancel{A}, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment})}_{\substack{\textbf{Measurement model} \\ (A \text{ carries no additional information about } Y_2)}} \\[0.5em]
&\quad \times \underbrace{P(Y_1 \mid A, \cancel{\text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}})}_{\substack{\textbf{Imputation model} \\ (\text{randomization})}}
\end{aligned}
\]

\(P(Y_1 \mid A)\) is the same in both Pretest groups, so the pretested group shows how \(A\) predicts \(Y_1\)
Missing (unpretested group) \(Y_1\) are drawn from plausible values given both \(A\) and \(Y_2\):

\[
P(Y_{1,\text{mis}} \mid Y_2, A, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}) \;\propto\;
P(Y_2 \mid Y_1, \text{Pretest}, \text{Treatment}) \times P(Y_1 \mid A)
\]

\(A\) must be measured before randomization and strongly related to \(Y_1\)

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Simulation Design

\[
\text{Math Score}_i = {} \beta_0 + \beta_1 (\text{Treatment}_i) + \beta_2 (\text{Baseline}_i) + \beta_3 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i) + \beta_4 (\text{Pretest}_i) \\[0.5em]
+ \underbrace{\beta_5 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)}_{\text{Manipulated}} + \beta_6 (\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i) + \underbrace{\beta_7 (\text{Treatment}_i)(\text{Pretest}_i)(\text{Baseline}_i)}_{\text{Manipulated}} + \varepsilon_{i,2}
\]
\[
A_{ik} \sim N(0, 1), \qquad
\text{Baseline}_i = \frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K} A_{ik} + \varepsilon_{i,1}}{\sqrt{K + \sigma_{B}^2}}, \qquad
\varepsilon_{i,1} \sim N(0, \sigma_{B}^2) , \qquad
\varepsilon_{i,2} \sim N(0, 1)
\]

\(N =\) 450, \(K =\) 3 auxiliary variables, \(R^2_{A} =\) 0.33
\(P(\text{Pretest}_i = 1) =\) 0.33, \(P(\text{Treatment}_i = 1) =\) 0.5
\(\beta_0 = 0,\ \beta_1 = 0.5,\ \beta_2 = 1,\ \beta_3 = -0.25,\ \beta_4 = 0.2,\ \beta_6 = 0\)

\(\beta_1\) implies medium treatment effect, \(\beta_3\) implies baseline offsets treatment

Crossed: \(\beta_5 \in \{0, -0.5\} \times \beta_7 \in \{0, 0.25\}\)
4 conditions, 200 replications each

title: Combatting Measurement Reactivity in Experimental Design and Inference
text:
Take Home


Between subjects designs are well powered for treatment effect but cannot detect reactivity or moderation effects
Mixed designs are very risky! Can trigger measurement reactivity, biasing treatment effects
Solomon ANOVA can detect measurement reactivity, but less powerfully than planned missing approaches, and cannot detect moderation
Planned missing designs with auxiliary variables simultaneously address these problems:

Test whether measurement reactivity is present, and if so
Recover unbiased treatment effects
Permit varying levels of treatment effect by baseline/trait ability (moderation)

Power weak at this \(N\) + effect size (more informative \(A\) might help), but recovery unbiased

ML (as implemented) less consistent than MI or Bayes
